title: The Law of the Spirit of Life
english: …human mind to endure, while evil is ranged against it. He insisted that the mind of the more upright is at times distressed when it is tyrannized by the passions of the flesh, that it is deeply troubled and ashamed of its weakness; yet it has no means at all of throwing off the burden of the sin it does not want, since pleasure falls upon it so fiercely. That is why it is too weak to resist, receiving no help whatever toward this, at least from the law.

So the inspired Paul speaks the truth when he insists that with the mind he serves the divine law, but with the flesh the law of sin (Romans 7:25); and this, I think, is what he meant when he said, “For willing lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good does not” (Romans 7:18). Formerly, then, as I said, so far as the mind and the will within it were concerned, we had the choice to serve the divine law; but the flesh forced us toward sin, raising up its own will in opposition, as it were. So there was, then, condemnation for those who wished to accomplish the good but were not able, because they were tyrannized by the passions; but in Christ what condemned has come to an end, that is, the domination of the fleshly impulses.

“For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:2). To make the ideas in these words perfectly clear, I think it necessary to say this: just as he calls the fleshly way of thinking, which carries us off toward every kind of wickedness, the law of sin and death, so he calls the spiritual will, that is, the mind’s inclination toward the good, the law of the spirit of life. But “the one who sows to the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, while the one who sows to the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Galatians 6:8).

So the law of the spirit of life, that is, the will of the mind that carries us toward life, was in us even before, for with the mind we served the law of God; but, as I said, it was sick, powerless to resist, and, overcome by the desires of the flesh, it was condemned by the law. But since it has cast off its sickness and been made strong through Christ — for through him we have been sealed with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13) and have been clothed with “power from on high” (Luke 24:49) — for this reason we have been redeemed and are no longer yoked to evil, but, as I said, we have been called to the dignity of freedom.

So the law of the spirit of life, that is, the will of the mind, which inclines toward doing good and carries us toward life, once it has been enriched with the grace that comes through Christ and set free from its ancient weakness, then, disregarding the evils that come from sin and prevailing over the law of the flesh, “has set me free,” he says (Romans 8:2). Not that it gives the freedom by itself, of course; rather, it has become for us the one who procures the freedom that comes through Christ. And just as those under the law of sin must, by every necessity, also be bound in the snares of death, so those who have come out from sin and been set free through Christ must in turn be beyond death, be seen to be above corruption, and live in holiness.

translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).
Section opens mid-sentence, continuing the last sentence of u05-rem-close (… τὴν | ἀνθρώπου διάνοιαν); rendered with a leading ellipsis.

τὸ ἀδύνατον τοῦ νόμου (Romans 8:3): rendered 'the law's inability' rather than 'what the law could not do', because Cyril goes on to gloss it as τὸ ἀσθενοῦν, 'the weakness', and argues that the sentence lacks a main verb.
κεκλήμεθα… εἰς ἐλεύθερον ἀξίωμα may echo Galatians 5:13 (ἐπ' ἐλευθερίᾳ ἐκλήθητε); possible allusion only, so not cited inline. Cyril marks it 'as I said', pointing back to his own earlier wording.
τοῖς τοῦ θανάτου… βρόχοις ('snares of death') is close to the Psalms' language (e.g. Psalm 18:5, LXX 17:6, which reads ὠδῖνες/παγίδες), but the wording does not match; not cited.
Page numbers 210 and 211 are edition apparatus and are omitted.
Section ends mid-sentence (Ἀξιάγαστος μὲν ὁ | μυσταγωγός…); the sentence continues at the start of u06-rem-early.

τό γε ἧκον εἰς νοῦν καὶ τὴν ἐν αὐτῷ θέλησιν is adverbial ('so far as the mind and its will were concerned'), with τὸ ἑλέσθαι … δουλεύειν as the subject of ἐνυπῆρχεν; πάλαι here means before Christ, so 'formerly' / 'even before' rather than 'long ago'.
κατεβιάζετο … ἡ σάρξ is middle with active sense, as in u05-rem-mid (καταβιάζεται … τὸν νοῦν); the unexpressed object is us (ἡμῖν above), so 'the flesh forced us toward sin'.
τὸ σαρκικὸν φρόνημα rendered 'the fleshly way of thinking' so it is not confused with νοῦς ('mind'), which this passage sets against the flesh.
in τοὺς ἔξω γεγονότας αὐτῆς the feminine αὐτῆς refers to sin (ἁμαρτίας), not to the masculine νόμον; rendered 'come out from sin'.

Spirit/spirit: in Romans 8:2 and Galatians 6:8 Cyril reads πνεῦμα as the spiritual will of the human mind (τὸ θέλημα τὸ πνευματικόν), its inclination toward the good, so 'spirit' is printed lowercase; the Holy Spirit, named separately, is capitalised.
